question: A 34-year-old man presents with multiple painful ulcers on his penis. He says that the ulcers all appeared suddenly at the same time 3 days ago. He reports that he is sexually active with multiple partners and uses condoms inconsistently. He is afebrile and his vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination reveals multiple small shallow ulcers with an erythematous base and without discharge. There is significant inguinal lymphadenopathy present. Which of the following is the most likely etiologic agent of this patient’s ulcers?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Multiple painful ulcers on the penis" -> "Sudden appearance of ulcers" -> "Consistent with a viral infection" -> "Inguinal lymphadenopathy present" -> "Herpes simplex virus is a common cause" -> 85%

CHAIN: "Multiple painful ulcers on the penis" -> "Ulcers with an erythematous base" -> "No discharge present" -> "Inguinal lymphadenopathy suggests an infectious etiology" -> "Herpes simplex virus is likely" -> 90%

CHAIN: "Patient is sexually active with multiple partners" -> "Inconsistent condom use increases risk of STIs" -> "Sudden onset of ulcers" -> "Herpes simplex virus commonly presents this way" -> "Other options less likely due to presentation" -> 80%

CHAIN: "Multiple shallow ulcers on the penis" -> "Significant inguinal lymphadenopathy" -> "Herpes simplex virus can cause this presentation" -> "Other STIs typically have different characteristics" -> 75%
enhanced_information: The patient presents with multiple painful ulcers on the penis, which appeared suddenly and are accompanied by significant inguinal lymphadenopathy. This presentation is highly suggestive of a herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection, as HSV commonly causes painful genital ulcers and can lead to lymphadenopathy. The presence of shallow ulcers with an erythematous base and without discharge further supports this diagnosis, as these characteristics align with HSV rather than other sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Other options, such as Treponema pallidum (syphilis) and Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid), typically present with different ulcer characteristics or systemic symptoms. The evidence paths indicating that ulcers can be manifestations of infections and that HSV is a common cause of such presentations reinforce the likelihood of HSV as the etiologic agent in this case.
analysis: The patient presents with multiple painful ulcers on the penis that appeared suddenly, along with significant inguinal lymphadenopathy. This clinical picture is highly suggestive of a herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection. HSV is known to cause painful genital ulcers, and the presence of shallow ulcers with an erythematous base aligns with typical HSV lesions. Other options such as Treponema pallidum (syphilis) and Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid) have different ulcer characteristics or systemic symptoms. For instance, syphilis typically presents with a single painless ulcer (chancre), and chancroid usually presents with larger, painful ulcers that may have purulent discharge. Given the acute onset, painful nature of the ulcers, and associated lymphadenopathy, HSV is the most likely etiologic agent in this case. Therefore, the best-supported option is herpes simplex virus.
